overview: groupBy in PySpark partitions a DataFrame into groups by one or more keys and applies aggregate functions to each group via groupBy().agg(), collapsing each group into a single output row.
Because rows for the same key must be brought together, groupBy triggers a shuffle, but Spark first performs partial (map-side) aggregation so only compact partial states cross the network.

groupBy collapses rows (one row per group) and differs from window aggregation, which keeps every row while adding an aggregate column; pivot() further reshapes grouped results from long to wide form.
learningObjectives: Use groupBy().agg() with single and multiple grouping keys and understand the resulting grain.
Explain the shuffle groupBy triggers and how partial aggregation / map-side combine reduce it.
Distinguish groupBy (collapsing) from window aggregation (non-collapsing) and use pivot() to reshape results.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: groupBy is a transformation that partitions a DataFrame's rows into groups defined by the distinct values of one or more grouping columns; a subsequent agg() applies aggregate functions to each group, producing exactly one output row per distinct combination of grouping keys.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: groupBy is like sorting a pile of receipts into stacks - one stack per store, or per store-and-day - and then summarizing each stack: total sales, number of receipts, and so on. You end up with one summary line per stack instead of all the individual receipts.
coreConcept.historicalContext: groupBy mirrors SQL's GROUP BY, rooted in relational algebra. In distributed engines the challenge is co-locating same-key rows, historically done with a reduce-side shuffle in MapReduce. Spark adds map-side combine (partial aggregation) to shrink the shuffle, and modern Spark uses HashAggregate with Tungsten code generation plus AQE to coalesce and skew-split post-shuffle partitions.

whyItMatters.business: Group-level summaries - sales per region, users per cohort, errors per service - are the core of reporting and KPIs. groupBy is how raw rows become the grouped metrics a business consumes.
whyItMatters.engineering: groupBy is the most common shuffle-inducing operation after joins. Understanding its shuffle, partial aggregation, and skew behavior is essential for performant aggregation pipelines.
whyItMatters.scalability: Partial aggregation lets groupBy scale to huge datasets by reducing data before the shuffle, but high group cardinality or skewed keys can still stress the cluster.
whyItMatters.cost: The shuffle is the dominant cost; reducing pre-shuffle data via map-side combine, filtering, and projecting directly lowers cluster runtime and spend.
whyItMatters.reliability: A single hot group concentrates work on one reducer task, causing stragglers or OOM; recognizing and handling group skew keeps jobs stable.

coreComponents.name: Grouping Keys
coreComponents.definition: The one or more columns passed to groupBy that define how rows are partitioned into groups.
coreComponents.purpose: Determine the grain of the output - one row per distinct combination of key values.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Define the hash used to shuffle rows so same-key rows land in the same partition.

coreComponents.name: agg() on GroupedData
coreComponents.definition: The method applied after groupBy that specifies the aggregate functions computed per group.
coreComponents.purpose: Collapse each group into a single summary row with the requested measures.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Apply sum/avg/count/etc per group and emit one row per group.

coreComponents.name: pivot()
coreComponents.definition: An operator between groupBy and agg that turns distinct values of a column into separate output columns, reshaping long data into wide form.
coreComponents.purpose: Produce a cross-tab where each pivot value becomes a column of aggregated measures.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Enumerate (or be given) the pivot values and aggregate per (group, pivot value) cell.

internalWorking: Spark plans groupBy().agg() as a HashAggregate with a partial phase and a final phase separated by a shuffle (an Exchange) on the grouping keys.
In the partial phase each partition computes per-key partial aggregates locally (map-side combine), so only one partial state per key per partition is produced.
The shuffle (hash partitioning by the grouping key) redistributes these partial states so all states for a key land in the same reducer partition.
The final phase merges the partial states per key into the final aggregate and emits one row per group; AQE may coalesce small post-shuffle partitions or split skewed ones at runtime.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: DataFrame -> partial aggregate per partition (map-side combine on grouping key) -> shuffle/Exchange by grouping key -> final aggregate merge per key -> one row per group (AQE may coalesce/skew-split partitions)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. df.groupBy("region").agg(F.sum("amount")) is executed on a DataFrame spread across many partitions.
2. Each partition computes a partial sum of amount per region it contains (map-side combine).
3. Spark shuffles these partial sums, hash-partitioning by region so all partial sums for 'US' land together.
4. The final aggregate adds the partial sums per region to get each region's total.
5. The result is one row per region; without map-side combine, all raw rows would have been shuffled instead of small partial sums.

keyTerminology.meaning: The hash-partitioning of data by the grouping key so same-key rows/states meet in one partition.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the main cost of groupBy; reducing pre-shuffle data is the key optimization.

keyTerminology.meaning: Computing per-partition partial aggregates before the shuffle so only compact partial states are sent.
keyTerminology.importance: Turns a full data shuffle into a tiny partial-state shuffle for reducible aggregates like sum/count.

keyTerminology.meaning: The number and granularity of groups; one output row per distinct grouping-key combination.
keyTerminology.importance: High cardinality means many small groups; skewed cardinality means a few huge groups that bottleneck reducers.

keyTerminology.meaning: Reshaping grouped data so distinct values of a column become separate aggregated columns (cross-tab).
keyTerminology.importance: Provides wide-format summaries but requires scanning to find pivot values unless they are supplied.

importantConcepts.explanation: groupBy().agg() returns one row per group (rows are collapsed). A window aggregation (F.sum over Window.partitionBy) computes the same per-group aggregate but attaches it to every original row, preserving row-level detail.

importantConcepts.concept: Multiple grouping keys define a finer grain
importantConcepts.explanation: groupBy("region", "category") groups by the combination, producing one row per (region, category) pair. More keys mean more, smaller groups and a finer-grained output.

importantConcepts.concept: Supplying pivot values avoids an extra scan
importantConcepts.explanation: df.groupBy(...).pivot("col", ["A","B","C"]) lets Spark skip the job it would otherwise run to discover distinct pivot values, making pivots faster and deterministic in column order.

variationsAndTypes: **Multi-key groupBy:** group by a combination of columns (groupBy("region", "category")).
**groupBy + pivot:** reshape long results into a wide cross-tab.
**Rollup / cube:** rollup() and cube() produce hierarchical and all-combination subtotals beyond a plain groupBy.
**grouping sets:** custom combinations of grouping columns via SQL GROUPING SETS for flexible subtotals.
advantages: **Scalable via map-side combine:** reducible aggregates shuffle only small partial states.
**Expressive:** supports arbitrary grouping keys, many measures, pivots, rollups, and cubes.
**Declarative:** Catalyst optimizes the aggregate plan and AQE tunes partitions at runtime.
**Composable:** integrates with the full aggregate-function library and conditional aggregation.
disadvantages: **Mandatory shuffle:** groupBy always exchanges data on the key, the dominant cost.
**Skew sensitivity:** a hot group lands on one reducer task and can straggle or OOM.
**Collapses detail:** loses row-level information, unlike window aggregation.
**Pivot scan cost:** discovering pivot values triggers an extra job unless values are supplied.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use groupBy().agg() when you need summary rows per key and row-level detail is not required. Use pivot() for wide cross-tab reports. Pre-aggregate before joins to shrink data.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid groupBy when you must retain every row alongside the aggregate (use a window instead). Avoid pivots without supplied values on high-cardinality pivot columns. Avoid plain groupBy on heavily skewed keys without AQE/salting.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: groupBy is like a teacher sorting exam papers into stacks by class and recording one summary line per class (average score, count). A window aggregation is like writing each student's class average next to their own paper, keeping every paper. A pivot is like turning that summary into a grid with one column per exam date.

commonMisconceptions.myth: groupBy sends all rows over the network.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For reducible aggregates Spark performs map-side combine first, so only compact partial states (one per key per partition) are shuffled, not the raw rows.

commonMisconceptions.myth: groupBy and window aggregation produce the same output.
commonMisconceptions.reality: groupBy collapses rows to one per group; a window aggregation keeps all rows and adds the aggregate as a new column. They serve different needs.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Map-side combine makes reducible groupBy scale well; cost grows with group cardinality and with non-reducible measures (collect_list). High-cardinality grouping inflates the number of output rows and shuffle partitions.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Group skew is the top failure mode: one hot key concentrates on a single reducer, causing stragglers or OOM. Enable AQE skew handling and consider salting or two-stage aggregation for hot keys.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Aggregation recomputes from lineage on task loss; the small partial-state shuffle speeds recovery, and the external shuffle service preserves shuffle files across executor restarts.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Inspect the final aggregate stage in the Spark UI for one long-running task (skew) and for spill; track output row count against expected group cardinality.
productionConsiderations.security: Grouping by sensitive attributes can create small groups that risk re-identification; apply minimum-group-size thresholds or masking when grouping regulated data.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Filter and project before grouping, compute all measures in one agg(), and enable AQE partition coalescing to avoid tiny output partitions; pre-aggregate before joins.
productionConsiderations.performance: Supply pivot values to skip the discovery scan, prefer reducible aggregates, and tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (or rely on AQE) so the post-shuffle partition count matches the group cardinality.

codeExamples.title: Single-key and multi-key groupBy with multiple measures
codeExamples.overview: Groups by one key, then by two keys, computing several aliased aggregates in one pass each.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("groupby").getOrCreate()

sales = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("US", "books", "Q1", 250.0), ("US", "books", "Q2", 75.0),
     ("US", "toys", "Q1", 400.0), ("UK", "books", "Q1", 120.0),
     ("UK", "toys", "Q2", 60.0)],
    ["region", "category", "quarter", "amount"],
)

# Single grouping key -> one row per region
by_region = sales.groupBy("region").agg(
    F.sum("amount").alias("total"),
    F.avg("amount").alias("avg_amt"),
    F.count("*").alias("n_sales"),
)
by_region.orderBy("region").show()

# Multiple grouping keys -> one row per (region, category)
by_region_cat = sales.groupBy("region", "category").agg(
    F.sum("amount").alias("total")
)
by_region_cat.orderBy("region", "category").show()
codeExamples.breakdown: groupBy("region") yields one row per region; groupBy("region", "category") yields one row per (region, category) combination, a finer grain. Both compute their measures in a single agg() pass with map-side combine, so only partial sums/counts are shuffled.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: by_region: US total=725.0 n_sales=3, UK total=180.0 n_sales=2. by_region_cat: (US,books)=325.0, (US,toys)=400.0, (UK,books)=120.0, (UK,toys)=60.0.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that adding a grouping key changes the grain and the row count; not aliasing measures; expecting row-level detail to survive (it is collapsed).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Project only the columns you group by and aggregate before calling groupBy to shrink the shuffle; compute all measures in one agg().

codeExamples.title: Pivot: long to wide cross-tab
codeExamples.overview: Uses groupBy().pivot().agg to turn quarter values into columns, with and without supplying pivot values.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Pivot quarters into columns: one row per region, columns Q1/Q2 of summed amount
wide = sales.groupBy("region").pivot("quarter").sum("amount")
wide.orderBy("region").show()

# Supply pivot values to skip the discovery scan and fix column order
wide_fast = (
    sales.groupBy("region")
    .pivot("quarter", ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"])
    .sum("amount")
)
wide_fast.orderBy("region").show()
codeExamples.breakdown: pivot("quarter") groups by region and turns each distinct quarter into its own column of summed amount, a cross-tab. Without a value list Spark runs an extra job to discover the distinct quarters; supplying ["Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4"] skips that scan and fixes the column order (unmatched values become null columns).
codeExamples.expectedOutput: wide: region, Q1, Q2 columns. US: Q1=650.0 (250+400), Q2=75.0. UK: Q1=120.0, Q2=60.0. wide_fast adds null Q3/Q4 columns.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Pivoting a high-cardinality column creates a huge, sparse output and an expensive discovery scan; not supplying values makes column order non-deterministic.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always supply the pivot value list when known; restrict pivots to low-cardinality columns; filter to the needed pivot values before pivoting.

codeExamples.title: groupBy (collapsing) vs window aggregation (non-collapsing)
codeExamples.overview: Shows the same per-group total computed two ways: groupBy collapses rows, a window keeps every row.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# groupBy: one row per region (detail is lost)
collapsed = sales.groupBy("region").agg(
    F.sum("amount").alias("region_total")
)
collapsed.show()  # 2 rows

# window: every original row kept, with region_total added as a new column
w = Window.partitionBy("region")
with_total = sales.withColumn("region_total", F.sum("amount").over(w))
with_total.orderBy("region", "category").show()  # 5 rows

# Common use: compute each sale's share of its region total (needs row-level detail)
with_share = with_total.withColumn(
    "share", F.col("amount") / F.col("region_total")
)
with_share.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: groupBy collapses the five sales rows into two region rows. The window version partitions by region but keeps all five rows, adding region_total to each, which enables row-level calculations like each sale's share of its region total - something groupBy alone cannot do without a join back.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: collapsed: 2 rows (US=725.0, UK=180.0). with_total: 5 rows each carrying its region_total. with_share: each row's amount/region_total.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using groupBy then joining back to regain row detail (slower) when a window would do it in one step; forgetting that windows do not reduce row count and can be memory-heavy on large partitions.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use groupBy when you only need summaries; use a window when you must keep every row alongside the aggregate (avoids an extra join).

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retailer needs a regional sales report: total and average sales plus order counts per region and category, presented as a wide quarter-by-quarter cross-tab, computed over a billion-row sales table.
endToEndExample.inputData: sales (region, category, quarter, customer_id, amount) ~1 billion rows in Parquet.
endToEndExample.architecture: PySpark on Spark 3.x with AQE enabled. A multi-key groupBy().agg() builds the summary; a separate groupBy().pivot() with supplied quarter values builds the cross-tab. Output written as Parquet partitioned by region.
processingSteps: 1. Read sales and project only the columns needed for grouping and aggregation to shrink the shuffle.
2. groupBy("region", "category").agg(sum, avg, count) - map-side combine reduces data before the Exchange.
3. Build the cross-tab with groupBy("region").pivot("quarter", ["Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4"]).sum("amount"), supplying values to skip the discovery scan.
4. Enable AQE to coalesce small post-shuffle partitions and split any skewed region partition.
5. Write the summary and the cross-tab to Parquet partitioned by region.
endToEndExample.output: A region-category summary table (region, category, total, avg_amt, n_sales) and a wide quarter cross-tab (region, Q1..Q4).
endToEndExample.monitoring: Inspect the final aggregate stage for a single long task (a hot region) and for spill; confirm output row count equals the number of (region, category) combinations.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a region is heavily skewed, enable AQE skew handling or apply two-stage (salted) aggregation; guard the pivot against unexpected high-cardinality quarter values by supplying the explicit list.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A cost-efficient report where map-side combine keeps the multi-key groupBy scalable, supplied pivot values avoid an extra scan, and AQE keeps partitions balanced under regional skew.

industryUseCases.problem: Produce daily sales summaries per store and category and quarter-over-quarter cross-tabs for merchandising.
industryUseCases.solution: Multi-key groupBy().agg() for summaries plus groupBy().pivot("quarter") for cross-tabs, with supplied pivot values.
industryUseCases.benefits: One-pass, partially-aggregated summaries scale to billions of rows, and pivots deliver ready-to-read wide reports.

industryUseCases.problem: Aggregate error and latency metrics per service and endpoint over high-volume log streams.
industryUseCases.solution: groupBy(service, endpoint).agg(count, avg(latency)) with AQE skew handling for hot endpoints.
industryUseCases.benefits: Map-side combine minimizes the shuffle; AQE balances partitions when a single endpoint dominates traffic.

industryUseCases.problem: Summarize transaction volume and value per merchant and per merchant-day for settlement reporting.
industryUseCases.solution: groupBy(merchant_id, day).agg(sum(amount), count) feeding settlement, with windows where per-transaction running totals are also needed.
industryUseCases.benefits: Deterministic per-key summaries at scale, with windows reserved for cases that must keep transaction-level detail.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Reducible groupBy scales via map-side combine, shuffling only partial states; scalability is bounded by group cardinality (number of output rows / shuffle partitions) and by non-reducible measures. AQE coalesces small partitions and splits skewed ones to keep tasks balanced.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Aggregation recomputes lost partitions from lineage; the compact partial-state shuffle speeds recovery, and the external shuffle service retains shuffle files across executor restarts.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: groupBy runs within one application; availability depends on the cluster manager and driver. Checkpoint before very heavy grouped aggregations to avoid recomputing long lineages after failures.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Grouping logic is reproducible code; recovery centers on input availability and idempotent output. Partitioned overwrite-by-key writes let a failed report job re-run safely.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Filter and project before grouping, compute all measures in one agg(), supply pivot values to skip the discovery scan, tune shuffle partition count (or rely on AQE), and pre-aggregate before joins to shrink data.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Map-side combine plus AQE partition coalescing minimizes shuffle volume and avoids tiny output partitions; pre-aggregation before joins and projection before the shuffle cut executor-hours.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Grouping on sensitive attributes can yield tiny groups that risk re-identification; enforce minimum-group-size suppression and mask sensitive keys when grouping regulated data.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use the Spark UI to detect a single long final-aggregate task (group skew) and disk spill; emit metrics on output cardinality and on shuffle read/write sizes to validate the grouping.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Confirm the output row count equals expected group cardinality, check for unexpected null grouping keys (they form their own group), and validate that pivot columns match the supplied value list.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Alert on executor OOM or excessive spill in the aggregate stage (often group skew or a runaway collector) and log shuffle partition counts and pivot value lists for reproducibility.

recommendedPractices: **Filter and project first:** reduce rows and columns before groupBy to shrink the shuffle.
**One agg() pass:** compute all measures together and alias each.
**Supply pivot values:** pass the value list to pivot() to skip the discovery scan and fix column order.
**Enable AQE:** let adaptive execution coalesce small partitions and handle group skew.
engineeringStandards: Be explicit about the output grain (which keys define a group) in code and documentation.
Prefer windows over groupBy + self-join when row-level detail must be retained.
Tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (or rely on AQE) so post-shuffle partitions match group cardinality.
designRecommendations: Pre-aggregate with groupBy before joining large tables to reduce join input size.
Limit pivots to low-cardinality columns; use rollup/cube/grouping sets for hierarchical subtotals.
Use two-stage (salted) aggregation for known hot keys to spread reducer load.
namingConventions: Alias grouped measures with descriptive snake_case names (region_total, n_sales).
Name pivot output columns predictably by supplying an ordered value list.
documentationStandards: Document the grouping keys and grain of each aggregated table.
Record the pivot column and its expected value set.
Note skew-handling strategy (AQE, salting) for hot groups.
testingStrategies: Unit-test groupBy on small fixtures asserting one row per group with known totals.
Test multi-key grouping changes the grain and row count as expected.
Test pivots with supplied values, including a value that produces a null column.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using groupBy then joining back to the original to regain row-level detail.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Needing both the aggregate and every row, but reaching for groupBy first.
commonMistakes.impact: An extra expensive join/shuffle that a single window aggregation would avoid.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a window aggregation (sum over Window.partitionBy) to attach the per-group value to every row in one pass.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pivoting a high-cardinality column without supplying values.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Not realizing pivot runs a discovery job and that many distinct values create a huge sparse table.
commonMistakes.impact: An extra scan, non-deterministic column order, and a wide, memory-heavy output.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Supply an explicit pivot value list and restrict pivots to low-cardinality columns.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring group skew on a hot key.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming groupBy parallelism is automatically balanced.
commonMistakes.impact: One reducer task straggles or OOMs while others finish, dominating runtime.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Enable AQE skew handling or use two-stage salted aggregation to spread the hot key across tasks.

comparisonSection.explanation: groupBy collapses each group into a single summary row, losing row-level detail. A window aggregation computes the same per-group value but keeps every original row, adding the aggregate as a new column - ideal when you need detail plus the summary (e.g. each row's share of its group total).

Reducible aggregates use map-side combine, shuffling only small partial states per key, so the shuffle stays compact. Collectors cannot reduce locally and must shuffle all values, producing a far larger shuffle and risking OOM on big groups.

Plain groupBy produces long-format rows (one per group, measures as columns). pivot reshapes distinct values of a column into separate columns (a cross-tab), useful for reports but costing a discovery scan and producing sparse wide output on high-cardinality pivot columns.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does groupBy().agg() return, and how does adding a second grouping key change the result?
beginnerQuestions.answer: groupBy("region").agg(...) returns one row per distinct region. Adding a key, groupBy("region", "category"), returns one row per distinct (region, category) combination - a finer grain with more rows.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Anchor on the grain: one output row per distinct combination of grouping keys. More keys means more, smaller groups.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you compute the total sales per region in PySpark?
beginnerQuestions.answer: df.groupBy("region").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("region_total")). This groups rows by region and sums amount within each group, returning one row per region.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show the alias for a clean column name and note that the original rows are collapsed.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between groupBy aggregation and window aggregation?
intermediateQuestions.answer: groupBy collapses each group into one summary row, losing row-level detail. A window aggregation (F.sum over Window.partitionBy) computes the same per-group value but keeps every original row, adding the aggregate as a new column. Use groupBy for summaries and a window when you need each row plus its group aggregate (e.g. a row's share of the group total).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize collapsing vs non-collapsing and the practical use case of avoiding a self-join.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is pivot() and what should you watch out for?
intermediateQuestions.answer: pivot() turns distinct values of a column into separate aggregated columns, producing a wide cross-tab (e.g. groupBy(region).pivot(quarter).sum(amount)). Watch out for high-cardinality pivot columns (huge sparse output) and the extra discovery job Spark runs if you do not supply the pivot value list.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Stress supplying the value list to skip the scan and to fix deterministic column order.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the shuffle that groupBy triggers and how partial aggregation reduces its cost.
advancedQuestions.answer: groupBy must co-locate same-key rows, so Spark inserts a shuffle (Exchange) that hash-partitions data by the grouping key. To shrink it, Spark first runs a partial aggregate on each partition (map-side combine), computing one partial state per key per partition, so only those compact states are shuffled rather than all raw rows. The final phase merges the partial states per key.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Name the two-phase HashAggregate, the Exchange, and that map-side combine only works for reducible aggregates, not collectors.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you handle a groupBy that is slow because one group is far larger than the others?
advancedQuestions.answer: That is group skew: the hot key lands on a single reducer task that straggles or OOMs. First enable AQE (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled with skew handling) to split oversized partitions. If insufficient, use two-stage aggregation: salt the hot key with a random suffix and aggregate (partial sums per salted key), then strip the salt and aggregate again to combine, spreading the hot key's work across many tasks.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Lead with AQE, then two-stage salted aggregation. Note that more executors alone do not fix skew.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You need each transaction row to also show what percentage it represents of its customer's total spend. A teammate proposes groupBy(customer) then join back. Is there a better way?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The requirement keeps every row but needs a per-customer total. groupBy collapses rows and would require a join to reattach the total; a window keeps rows and adds the total directly.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Use a window aggregation: w = Window.partitionBy('customer_id'); df.withColumn('cust_total', F.sum('amount').over(w)).withColumn('pct', F.col('amount')/F.col('cust_total')). This keeps every transaction row and computes the percentage in one pass, avoiding the extra shuffle of a groupBy + self-join.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a daily report that produces per-store/per-category sales summaries and a wide month-by-month cross-tab over a high-volume sales table, optimizing for cost and stability.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Project needed columns, run a multi-key groupBy(store, category).agg(sum, avg, count) for summaries, and a separate groupBy(store).pivot('month', [Jan..Dec]).sum(amount) with supplied values for the cross-tab. Enable AQE and write partitioned by store.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Map-side combine keeps summaries cheap; pivots cost a wide output and would cost a discovery scan if values were not supplied. High store-category cardinality increases output rows and shuffle partitions.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Rely on AQE to coalesce small partitions and split skewed stores; pre-aggregate before any downstream join; tune shuffle partitions to match cardinality; apply two-stage salting if a single store dominates volume.

Which aggregates benefit from map-side combine and which do not?
How do rollup and cube differ from a plain groupBy?
What happens to null values in a grouping key?
How does supplying pivot values change Spark's execution?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: groupBy partitions a DataFrame by one or more keys and agg() collapses each group into one summary row, triggering a shuffle that partial (map-side) aggregation keeps compact; pivot() reshapes results to wide form and windows keep all rows.
keyConcepts: groupBy(keys).agg(...) returns one row per distinct key combination (collapses rows).
groupBy triggers a shuffle/Exchange on the grouping key.
Partial aggregation / map-side combine shuffles only small partial states for reducible aggregates.
Window aggregation computes the same per-group value but keeps every row.
pivot() turns column values into columns; supply values to skip the discovery scan.
formulas: Output rows = number of distinct grouping-key combinations (one row per group)
interviewPoints: groupBy collapses to one row per group; window keeps every row.
groupBy always shuffles on the key; map-side combine shrinks it.
Reducible aggregates (sum/count) combine map-side; collectors do not.
Supply pivot values to avoid an extra scan and fix column order.
Group skew = one hot reducer task; fix with AQE or two-stage salting.
quickNotes: More grouping keys = finer grain = more output rows.
Null grouping-key values form their own group.
Use a window instead of groupBy + self-join to keep row detail.
Filter/project before groupBy to shrink the shuffle.
rollup/cube/grouping sets add hierarchical subtotals beyond plain groupBy.

keyTakeaways: groupBy(keys).agg(...) collapses rows into one summary row per distinct key combination and triggers a shuffle (Exchange) on the grouping key, the dominant cost of the operation.

Spark performs partial (map-side) aggregation before the shuffle for reducible aggregates like sum and count, so only compact partial states cross the network; collectors like collect_list cannot reduce this way and shuffle far more.
groupBy is collapsing while window aggregation is non-collapsing: use a window when you need every row alongside its group aggregate to avoid an extra groupBy + self-join.
pivot() reshapes long results into a wide cross-tab; always supply the pivot value list to skip Spark's discovery scan, fix column order, and keep the output bounded.
Group skew - a single hot key on one reducer task - is the main reliability risk; resolve it with AQE skew handling or two-stage salted aggregation rather than just adding executors.
